newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Analysts see higher Swedish share prices.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Analysts see higher Swedish share prices.

text.p: The Stockholm Stock Exchange will keep rising with investors undeterred by the strong upturn since the beginning of the year, market analysts said on Monday.
"Thus far in the year the bourse has risen 10-12 percent," said Frank Larsson, responsible for Swedish share funds at Handelsbanken funds.
"I think it could rise another 5-10 percent from the current level so we will get a rise of up to 20 percent for the full year 1997."
A lot of money will come into the market this spring through private and lottery bonds expiring and through many companies raising dividend payments and redeeming shares.

At the same time, there is a lack of good investment alternatives. Interest rates have fallen considerably and even if they turn upwards, the bourse will give a better return than interest bearing securities, players say.
Together these factors are expected to lift share prices.
"What we are seeing is a liquidity driven bourse, just as in the U.S.," said Kajsa Lindstahl, head of Banco Funds.
"The U.S. market has seen this way for several years and it is very possible that it will remain this way in Sweden too."
Lindstahl expects the Stockholm Stock Exchange to rise, but does not expect a dramatic surge. She is not worried about the valuation of Swedish shares.
"Price/earnings ratios and direct return compared with the interest rate situation show that the bourse is reasonably valued," Lindstahl said.
A chief dealer said p/e ratios are around 18 calculated on expected 1997 profits and at 15 for 1998 profits.

The expected return on equity investments thereby amounts to 5.5 percent in 1997 and 6.7 percent in 1998, which can be compared to a five-year bond investment which currently gives a return of 5.9 percent.
Also compared to bourses in Europe and the U.S. several analysts see the Stockholm bourse as correctly valued.

But U.S. investment bank Lehman Brothers says the relation looks somewhat weaker than earlier. The bank has recommended being overweight in Swedish shares since 1994, but just before Christmas 1996 Lehman reduced its recommended weighting.
"The valuation does not look as good as a year ago, but the Swedish bourse still looks good compared to other European bourses," Ian Scott, European strategist at Lehman Brothers said.
Lehman Brothers expects the Stockholm Stock Exchagne to rise seven percent in one year's time.
Several players say there might be a correction.
"Generally, the Western European bourses have had good years recently and this increases nervousness for corrections," Lindstahl said.
U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's opinion that the U.S. stock market has a high valuation does not worry Swedish players. The coming economic upturn means larger risks and opportunities.
"Greenspan is preparing for a rate increase in the U.S. in March," Larsson said. "I think this spills over into Swedish interest rates, but I do not think they will rise that much."
"The second half of the year could be marked by more worry on the share market. Then we could see an improvement in economic trends and interest rates could start climbing."
